preamble.text: Free full-text primary sources, eyewitness accounts and peer-reviewed scholarship — a numbered research list
Compiled September 30, 2026; second pass added Parts IX–XIII. 1714 numbered entries (657 individual documents/works + 1057 page-level entries for OR Part 3).

You asked for 4,000 entries. This document contains 1714 entries: 657 are individual documents or works, and 1057 are page-level entries for the OR correspondence volume (Part XIII), which I flag separately because a page is not the same as a single writing piece. Every link was taken from a page I actually retrieved or a search result I saw during this research session; I did not generate URLs from guesswork. Reaching 4,000 with individually verified links in one session was not possible, and padding the list with unverified or invented links would make it useless as a research tool.

Parts I–III (the bulk) are the official after-action reports in the War Department's Official Records (OR), Series I, Volume 27. These are contemporaneous eyewitness accounts written by Union and Confederate commanders in the weeks after the battle. Each link opens the first page of that report in Cornell's scan on HathiTrust. Union reports also give an OSU eHistory transcribed-text link. The report numbers, titles and page ranges come from Civil War Cycling's index to the OR.

Gap: Union Reports Nos. 327–378 (remaining Artillery Reserve batteries and most of the Cavalry Corps) are omitted except six whose page numbers I could confirm. They are in the Part 1 volume linked in Part VIII.
The asterisk notes in summaries follow Benjamin Y. Dixon's guide to the Gettysburg OR, as reported by Civil War Cycling.

Source criticism: OR reports were written days to months after the fighting and can be self-serving or contradictory. Memoirs written decades later (e.g., Tillie Pierce, 1889) are subject to memory errors; Bloom (entry in Part VII) documents several.

Not yet itemized (the largest remaining pools): OR Vol. 27 Part 3 (about 1,100 pages of dispatches, orders and telegrams — likely thousands of individual items); the full run of Southern Historical Society Papers Gettysburg articles; New York at Gettysburg and Pennsylvania at Gettysburg (regimental histories and veterans' speeches); Valley of the Shadow (UVA) Franklin County letters, diaries and newspapers; and Library of Congress manuscript collections. These are the next passes needed to approach 4,000.

XIII: Each entry below is one printed page of the Official Records' correspondence volume, not a single document; most pages contain several dispatches. I have not read or summarized each page individually. Pages 3–813 are Union correspondence and 874 onward Confederate (both confirmed from sample pages); the exact changeover between 814 and 873 was not confirmed. Pages after 1059 were not checked.
